newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD 1997-98 growth seen at 2.5-3.0 percent - draft.
newsitem.headline: OECD 1997-98 growth seen at 2.5-3.0 percent - draft.

text.p: The OECD sees economic growth of 2-5-3.0 percent in 1997-98 and expects it to be more balanced across the 29 member countries, says a draft OECD communique being prepared for release at the end of a two-day meeting.

The draft obtained by Reuters on Monday also says that the pursuit of credible monetary and fiscal policies, combined with sound financial systems and structural reforms can help to avoid unnecessary volatility of interest and exchange rates.

"OECD countries generally have budget deficit or debt levels which are still too high and population ageing threatens to push up public spending further," says the draft, which OECD sources say is unlikely to change much before being published on Tuesday at the end of a two-day ministerial meeting here.
"Given high tax burdens in many countries, the main effort in cutting deficits will have to fall on expenditures," it says.

"Ministers noted that economic growth, projected to average 2.5 to 3 percent in 1997-98, seems likely to be more balanced across OECD countries. Inflation is low almost everywhere but unemployment remains high in many countries."

"Ministers welcomed the efforts of the European Union countries to ensure successful introduction of the euro (single currency) and a well-functioning EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union)," it says.
"They agreed that a successful EMU, underpinned by sound macroeconomic and structural policies, would contribute to the stability of the international monetary system," it said.
"Ministers confirmed their commitment to pursue sustainable non-inflationary growth.

"They recognised that transforming this growth into rising employment would require some differences in the short-run orientation of macro-economic policies to reflect countries' varying cyclical positions," the draft says.

"Ministers agreed that continued fiscal consolidation is an overriding macroeconomic policy need in most OECD countries over the next few years to create the conditions for sustained growth," it says.
A mixture of finance, trade, social and foreign affairs ministers are attending the meeting and devoted the first part of Monday to discussion of "globalisation", or increasingly international trade.

"Ministers underlined their conviction that globalisation offers a real opportunity to improve living standards in their own countries and to allow all countries to participate in world development," the draft says.
"The challenge for governments is to pursue policies whereby the benefits of globalisation are fully realised while those most adversely affected are assisted," it adds.
